longmont city council open forum airport noise and election reform take stage longmont in a wideranging threehour open forum on tuesday night the longmont city council heard from dozens of residents on issues ranging from the nuisance of flight school traffic at vance brand airport to a coordinated push for ranked choice voting in municipal elections the january 20 2026 meeting served as a barometer for civic sentiment characterized by council members as a civil and productive session while the council took no formal legislative action the meeting surfaced deepseated frustrations regarding local aviation and a burgeoning movement for systemic electoral change aviation concerns dominate public comment the primary focus of the evening was vance brand airport kmo over a dozen speakers many from unincorporated boulder county expressed exhaustion with what they described as a decimated quality of life due to an uptick in flight school operations over the last two years residents argued that the airport has shifted from a community asset to a training hub for outside flight schools primarily those based at the rocky mountain metropolitan airport rmma the flight schools have absolutely no respect for the longmont community said resident ek grafe rmma is listed as one of the most dangerous airports in the country so they send all their traffic to longmont to make us less safe recurring themes regarding the airport included lead pollution multiple speakers including keith hughes expressed alarm over the continued use of leaded aviation fuel avgas and its impact on children in schools under flight paths noise and pattern saturation residents like maria watson a 30year resident and mia french who lives at 65th and nelson testified that the noise has made it impossible to conduct outdoor business or enjoy their properties local authority several speakers including allison schultz and sandra luck challenged the assertion that the city is powerless against the federal aviation administration faa they cited a legal brief from a recent boulder county lawsuit arguing that airport proprietors have the power to abate nuisances through nondiscriminatory regulations council member matthew popkin the liaison to the airport advisory board informed the public that a rates and charges study is currently underway steve brinkman and others are righttraffic has increased popkin acknowledged a coordinated push for ranked choice voting a significant portion of the meeting was dedicated to a presentation by the group ranked choice voting for longmont the advocates argued for transitioning the city away from plurality voting which they claimed leads to votesplitting michael habinsky representing the group described the current system as punishing a vibrant democracy he was followed by gwen steele and dylan rankin who addressed common concerns about complexity rankin cited data from new york city and alaska stating that 95 of voters found ranked choice ballots easy to complete the push for reform was framed as a civil rights issue by andrew barton of colorado common cause barton argued that ranked choice voting ensures that the hispaniclatino population has a more reliable path to representation talmaner concluded the groups remarks by requesting a definitive date for a formal study session community identity and sundance base camp beyond aviation and elections residents proposed visionary uses for longmonts infrastructure resident mike schnatzmeyer pitched a strategy to leverage the sundance film festivals arrival in the region he proposed using the boulder county fairgrounds as a sundance base camp to showcase local technicians and makers chris alred and longmont public media would be natural partners in this schnatzmeyer suggested noting the potential for millions in local economic impact other residents called for better transit paul beard urged the council to demand direct rtd bus service to denver international airport dia noting longmonts size as the largest city in the county youth activities georginetta johnson an 81year resident advocated for an indoor ice skating and roller rink housing diversity dan sorrels of launch longmont and john lumpkin advocated for legalizing townhouses and accessory dwelling units adus to address a major housing deficit council response and next steps the evening concluded with rare cultural contributions strider benston a longtime local figure performed a song in honor of martin luther king jr week while resident meg thornbury encouraged the room to maintain community solidarity council members expressed gratitude for the civil tone of the evening council member crystal prieto noted her commitment to finding peace of mind for residents bothered by noise while council member alex kalkhofer expressed an eagerness to visit different parts of the city to understand resident concerns firsthand we hear our community and we are working on it said council member jake marsing these conversations really do shape where we go as a council the city council is expected to revisit the airport rates study and the ranked choice voting study session in late february and march

the hidden exit fees of living in a cheap state brookstone news jan 22 2026 for the past decade americans have been told a simple story about geography if your city is expensive move somewhere cheaper trade san francisco for austin new york for nashville california for florida lower taxes cheaper homes more breathing room on paper the math works but for a growing number of households the problem is not the cost of getting into a cheap state it is the cost of getting out we are slowly discovering that many lowcost regions impose something like exit fees invisible compounding costs that make staying risky and leaving difficult these fees are not written into any contract they appear as insurance shocks tax reassessments infrastructure charges and labor market traps they do not show up in costofliving calculators but they increasingly determine whether a household builds stability or gets stuck the insurance cliff the most obvious exit fee is insurance in much of the sun belt home insurance has become a floating expense premiums double or triple in a few years carriers exit entire counties deductibles rise coverage shrinks renewal notices arrive with numbers that wipe out raises and bonuses in a single line consider a household that moved to a coastal florida suburb in 2021 their mortgage is affordable their taxes are low they feel smart three years later their insurance has gone from 1800 a year to 7000 their deductible is now five percent of home value their carrier is on its third balancesheet restructuring selling is no longer simple buyers factor in the insurance risk lenders tighten terms prices soften just as carrying costs explode the household did not just buy a cheaper home they bought exposure this is the first exit fee volatility that reduces both cash flow and resale value at the same time property taxes that reset at the worst moment cheap states often advertise low property taxes what they do not advertise is how aggressively those taxes can reset in fastgrowing counties assessments rise quickly as budgets expand to fund schools roads and emergency services in fiscally stressed regions reassessments arrive suddenly to plug holes the effect is the same monthly housing costs jump not because the homeowner upgraded but because the local government did consider a family in a fastgrowing texas exurb they bought in 2020 fixedrate mortgage stable payment in 2024 the county reassesses their home 35 percent higher their tax bill rises by several hundred dollars a month their escrow adjusts upward their cheap mortgage quietly becomes expensive leaving is not costless selling triggers transaction fees buying elsewhere means todays interest rates renting means higher deposits and unstable leases this is the second exit fee fiscal volatility embedded in local government finance utilities infrastructure and the price of fragility in stable regions infrastructure costs are socialized quietly over decades in fastgrowing or climatestressed regions they arrive as line items grid reliability charges storm hardening fees water surcharges sewer assessments private utility monopolies passing through capital costs these charges are rarely predictable and almost never optional a household in arizona moves for cheap housing and sunshine three summers later the utility adds a new capacity recovery fee after rolling blackouts their summer bill doubles their air conditioning becomes a financial decision again leaving is harder than it sounds jobs are local kids are in school housing markets are thin this is the third exit fee infrastructure risk passed directly to households hoa fees and the privatization of local government in many lowtax states governance is quietly privatized roads drainage storm systems security and even utilities are managed by homeowner associations and special districts fees rise not through elections but through board votes and emergency assessments a couple buys into a masterplanned community outside phoenix the hoa fee is modest the amenities look attractive then the retaining walls fail the storm drains need upgrading the reserve fund is empty a 12000 special assessment arrives the home is harder to sell buyers see the fee history lenders hesitate the couple pays or defaults this is the fourth exit fee privatized governance with no political buffer labor market risk the trap beneath the cheap house the final exit fee is the most subtle cheap states often have thin labor markets concentrated in a few industries logistics construction tourism energy healthcare wages are lower job ladders are shorter switching employers is harder a household moves for lower housing costs and remote flexibility two years later their company mandates returntooffice local jobs pay twenty percent less their mortgage is cheap but their income options collapse they cannot easily move again their home is illiquid their savings are thin their career stalls this is the fifth exit fee income risk disguised as affordability the real cost of cheap none of these fees appear in relocation guides costofliving indexes compare groceries and gas they do not price volatility they do not model resale risk they do not ask how easy it is to reverse the decision but households feel the difference immediately in stable regions expenses are high but predictable in volatile regions expenses are lower but unstable one allows planning the other taxes attention savings and optionality this is why migration patterns now look strange people are not simply leaving expensive states they are leaving places where exit fees are rising faster than wages they are not chasing cheap they are chasing survivable the quiet redefinition of affordability affordability used to mean price today it increasingly means something else the ability to change your mind can you leave if your job changes can you sell if insurance explodes can you absorb a tax reset or infrastructure charge without destabilizing your life in the modern housing market the most valuable feature of a location is not low cost it is low friction the tragedy is that exit fees hit hardest where people moved seeking relief cheap states still attract millions of households many will thrive but an increasing number will discover that the real cost of cheap is not what you pay to arrive it is what you pay when you try to leave as always i read every reply and im genuinely curious where you land on this because how we interpret these structural forces matters almost as much as the numbers themselves
